subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Guided Practice — Dissociating Memory Systems in Amnesia

Scenario: Mr Patel, a 55-year-old patient, has recently been diagnosed with Korsakoff syndrome following chronic alcohol misuse and severe malnutrition. On formal neuropsychological testing, he cannot recall events from the past week, struggles to learn new word lists, and frequently produces confabulated accounts of events that did not occur. However, his vocabulary, mathematical ability, and the motor skills of his previous trade (carpentry) remain intact.

Using your knowledge of Korsakoff syndrome and Squire's (1992) memory systems taxonomy, identify which memory systems are impaired and which are preserved in Mr Patel's case. Explain the underlying neuroanatomy (referring to relevant diencephalic structures), and briefly compare his pattern to that observed in early Alzheimer's disease.

Guidance: Map each observed strength and difficulty onto a specific memory system. Aim for 110–130 words. Be precise about anatomy: name the structures involved.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Mr Patel exhibits a severe impairment in his declarative memory, specifically the episodic subsystem (manifesting as profound anterograde amnesia for recent events). His production of confabulated accounts further characterises this episodic failure. However, his non-declarative memory remains preserved, demonstrated by his intact procedural memory for carpentry. His remote semantic memory (vocabulary and mathematics) is also largely preserved.

This presentation arises from damage to diencephalic structures — notably the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus — caused by thiamine deficiency. While his behavioural profile (episodic memory loss with preserved procedural and remote semantic memory) is similar to early Alzheimer's disease, the underlying neuroanatomy differs. Early Alzheimer's is driven by tau pathology in the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus (Braak stages I–IV), whereas Korsakoff syndrome spares the hippocampus directly but destroys the critical diencephalic nodes of the extended memory network.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Evaluating the Neuroscience of Alzheimer's Disease

The amyloid cascade hypothesis (Hardy & Higgins, 1992) has guided much of Alzheimer's disease research for over three decades. Following the 2023 FDA approval of lecanemab and the 2024 approval of donanemab, some commentators have declared the amyloid hypothesis vindicated, while others remain sceptical of the clinical significance of these therapies.

Critically evaluate the contemporary status of the amyloid cascade hypothesis. Refer to Braak & Braak's (1991) staging of tau pathology, the relationship between neuropathology and clinical symptoms, and recent developments including plasma biomarkers (Bellaver et al., 2021) and amyloid-targeting therapies. Conclude with a justified assessment of whether the amyloid hypothesis adequately explains Alzheimer's disease and what alternative frameworks merit consideration.

Write at least 150 words. Construct a sustained evaluative argument in paragraph form. Cite named researchers and years throughout.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The amyloid cascade hypothesis, originally formulated by Hardy and Higgins (1992), proposed that the deposition of beta-amyloid plaques is the primary pathological trigger of Alzheimer's disease, with tau neurofibrillary pathology, synaptic dysfunction, neuronal loss, and clinical decline arising as downstream consequences. The hypothesis was attractive because it offered a unifying causal mechanism and identified a clear therapeutic target. For three decades it has guided drug development, with billions of dollars invested in amyloid-targeting therapies — most of which failed in clinical trials throughout the 2010s, prompting serious doubt.

The FDA approvals of lecanemab in 2023 and donanemab in 2024 have partially rehabilitated the hypothesis. Both monoclonal antibodies clear amyloid from the brain and produce modest but statistically significant slowing of cognitive decline in early Alzheimer's disease. However, the clinical significance of these effects is contested. The absolute differences from placebo are small, the risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA — cerebral oedema and microhaemorrhages) is non-trivial, and the cost is substantial. Critics argue that demonstrating biological target engagement is not the same as demonstrating clinically meaningful disease modification.

Several lines of evidence complicate a purely amyloid-centric account. Braak and Braak's (1991) staging of tau pathology shows that tau accumulation correlates more closely with cognitive decline than does amyloid burden. The clinical symptoms of early Alzheimer's — episodic memory loss reflecting hippocampal dysfunction — map directly onto tau pathology in the medial temporal lobe (Braak stages III–IV) rather than onto the diffuse cortical amyloid distribution. Many cognitively normal older adults have substantial amyloid deposits without dementia, while tau correlates more reliably with clinical severity. Bellaver et al.'s (2021) plasma p-tau181 biomarker work has shifted attention toward tau as a more sensitive predictor of disease progression.

Alternative frameworks merit serious consideration. Neuroinflammation, with microglial activation and complement-mediated synaptic loss, has emerged as a major contributor. Vascular factors and the gut–brain axis are increasingly investigated. The prion-like spread of tau between neurons offers a different mechanistic perspective on disease progression. A pluralistic view — that Alzheimer's disease arises from the convergence of amyloid, tau, inflammation, vascular dysfunction, and other factors — fits the evidence better than monocausal models. The amyloid hypothesis is not falsified, but it is now best understood as part of a broader pathological cascade rather than its sole driver. Tau-targeting therapies, combination treatments, and biomarker-guided early intervention represent the most promising current directions.
